stroke-width='1.2'/><text x='160' y='265.5' fill='#c9d4f2' font-size='8.4' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>🎣 patient dip order at next open</text></svg>Every 'no' is written to the diary with its reason — the machine never ghosts you. (Your numbers and settings may differ — the mechanics are the lesson.)
💧 The liquidity floor

Shares that barely trade are cut first. A pattern you can't actually buy or sell at a fair price is a mirage — the same floor the report card uses (lesson 29). Thin shares LOOK exciting precisely because tiny money moves them; that's the trap being filtered.
🎯 The source lane + /10 gate

The bot shops only from your chosen lane (🧪 Best proven scan by default, 🏆 Top 20, or another lens), then applies your Min Watch Score — the 'is someone quietly collecting this TODAY?' rating from lesson 33. Your gate, your choosiness: 4 = Building or better, 7 = Strong only.
📋 The proof gate — signals from YOUR card

With 🪜 Auto-follow on, the bot only buys shares showing the top-rated PROVEN lines from your report card — SOLID/PROMISING with positive edge, never a TOO-EARLY line — and its combo gate follows the card's best pairs. It re-reads the ladder every data day, so as flags prove or fade, the bot follows automatically. No re-ticking, no favourites.
🧭 The regime gate (the globe icon in your rules)

When the index sits below its own 50-day average, the market's tide is out — most shares fall regardless of merit. The gate simply pauses NEW buys in that weather and lets cash wait. Old positions still manage their exits; nothing panic-sells.
🚫 The don't-chase gates

Three questions that stop the bot buying excitement (lesson 15): is today actually green? is it not already overheated (RSI)? and did it NOT just leap a huge single-day jump? A setup is a beginning; a spike is usually an ending.
Sizing and the patience order

Only now does money enter: size from risk (the 1% rule — lesson 39), cap by 📦, respect the $500 minimum, check the cash. Then instead of paying any price, the bot places a 🎣 patient limit a touch below (default 2%, matching the tested presets, tunable per share with 📉 Dip Finder) at the next open — if the market never dips to meet it, the order simply expires. Missing a trade is free; overpaying isn't.
🔢 The last gates

Max open positions and max buys per day cap the whole machine — no burst of enthusiasm can concentrate your account in one lucky afternoon. What's left is a small, reasoned, fully-logged set of practice buys. Practice money only: this machine cannot touch a real broker. One more thing the funnel no longer needs: you. With the bot ON, your saved rules also run on the server at end-of-day — the same graded-evidence engine the backtests used, applying your band, score gate, dip entry and exits — and your next open places those decisions as dated practice orders, marked 🌐 in the diary. The local funnel stands down for any day the server already decided.

quiz.q: Why is the liquidity floor the FIRST gate?
a: A pattern you can't trade at a fair price is a mirage — everything downstream would be wasted on it
quiz.why: Thin shares look exciting because tiny money moves them. Cutting them first keeps every later judgement honest.

quiz.q: With 🪜 Auto-follow on, the bot's signal choices…
a: Re-read your report card every data day — as lines prove or fade, the bot follows
Include TOO-EARLY lines if the edge is big
quiz.why: The proof gate is adaptive and never trusts an unproven line, no matter how pretty its edge.

quiz.q: The 🎣 patient dip order means…
a: The bot pays whatever the open costs
A limit slightly below — if the market never dips to it, the order expires; missing a trade is free, overpaying isn't
Orders are placed at random times
quiz.why: Patience is a position: the bot would rather miss than chase.

quiz.q: When the regime gate is closed, the bot…
a: Pauses NEW buys and lets cash wait; existing positions still manage their exits normally
quiz.why: The gate manages weather, not positions — it stops adding risk in a falling tide without panic-selling what's aboard.

title: 38 · The five exits, drawn — and how they share the job
steps: Exits are the personality

Two bots with identical entries and different exits produce totally different lives. The app gives every position five exits that watch it simultaneously — whichever triggers first acts.  (Your numbers and settings may differ — the mechanics are the lesson.)
🛑 The hard stop — the floor

Set at buy time, a fixed percentage below entry (tick-rounded). It answers the only question that matters on day one: 'how much am I willing to be wrong?' Everything in sizing (lesson 39) is measured off this line.
🛡 The breakeven shield, then 🪤 the trail

Once the share is up a set amount, the shield lifts the stop to your ENTRY — from that moment a winner cannot become a loser. As it climbs further, the trailing stop follows a set percentage under the HIGHEST close — stepping up, never down, locking profit as it goes. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 134' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polyline points='10,92 50,84 90,88 130,72 170,62 210,66 250,48 305,40' fill='none' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='2.2'/><circle cx='10' cy='92' r='3.5' fill='#f5c84c'/><text x='18' y='99' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>buy</text><line x1='8' y1='114' x2='312' y2='114' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><text x='10' y='128' fill='#f87171' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>🛑 hard stop — the floor under day one</text><polyline points='8,102 130,102 130,88 210,88 210,68 305,68' fill='none' stroke='#f5c84c' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-dasharray='2 3'/><text x='148' y='80' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>🪤 trail — steps UP, never down</text><line x1='130' y1='94' x2='312' y2='94' stroke='#60a5fa' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><text x='150' y='106' fill='#60a5fa' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>🛡 shield — stop lifted to your entry</text></svg>The three lines are one story: floor first, then breakeven, then a rising floor that chases the price.
🎯 The target and the scale-out runner

At the target, the bot doesn't have to choose between 'take the money' and 'let it run' — scale-out sells PART (default half) and the remaining runner rides the trailing stop. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 110' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='8' y1='22' x2='312' y2='22' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='1.6' stroke-dasharray='6 4'/><text x='10' y='16' fill='#4ade80' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>🎯 target</text><polyline points='10,84 60,74 110,78 160,58 200,40 226,22' fill='none' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='2.2'/><circle cx='226' cy='22' r='4' fill='#4ade80'/><text x='148' y='34' fill='#4ade80' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>sell HALF here</text><polyline points='226,22 250,30 275,24 305,14' fill='none' stroke='#f5c84c' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='3 3'/><text x='238' y='46' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>the runner rides the 🪤 trail</text><text x='10' y='102' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>⏱ and if a share just drifts, the time exit frees the cash after N days</text></svg>Banked profit AND open upside. If the runner gets stopped later, the trade still ends green far more often.
⏱ The time exit

Some shares neither win nor lose — they just drift, tying up cash that could work elsewhere. After a set number of days, out. Dead money has a cost the ledger never shows: the trades you couldn't take.
The presets — three personalities

🛡 Defender: 🎯15 🛑15 on $0.20–$0.99 — banks early, right about two thirds of the time. ⚖ All-rounder: 🎯20 🛑15 on $0.20–$1.99 — the balance the lessons teach (band re-set on the ten-year test: the sub-20c tail and the old $1.75 ceiling were both costing it). ⚡ Hunter: no target and no fixed stop at all, a 🪤 20% trail alone on $0.20–$0.99 — +232% on the ten-year replay against +97% and +58% for the other two — measured with look-ahead in the signal scores AND only on companies still listed today (the dead ones aren’t in the data), so treat it as a ceiling, not an expectation. Honestly re-graded window by window it wins about a THIRD of its trades, not half, with ~9-week holds and 20% given back from every peak. See lesson 55. None is 'best'; they're different answers to how much pain buys how much possibility.
Who fires first?

A share can cross several lines in one day's move; the engine honours the protective order — stops protect before targets celebrate. And your 10d research view (lesson 31's '10d stronger than 5d') is exactly the evidence to watch when wondering whether trails deserve more room: if the drift keeps continuing past day 5 across weeks of cards, tight profit-taking is the leak.

quiz.q: After the 🛡 shield lifts the stop to entry…
a: The trade can still become a loser
The worst remaining outcome is breakeven — a winner can no longer turn into a loss
quiz.why: That's the shield's whole job: past +X%, the downside is capped at zero.

quiz.q: The 🪤 trailing stop moves…
a: Up and down with the price
Only UP — a set percentage under the highest close reached
quiz.why: Ratchet, not elastic: it follows the peak and never gives back what it's locked.

quiz.q: Scale-out at the 🎯 target means…
a: Sell part (default half), bank it, and let the runner ride the trail
quiz.why: It dissolves the take-profit-vs-let-it-run dilemma: some of both, by design.

quiz.q: The ⏱ time exit exists because…
a: Drifting shares tie up cash that could work elsewhere — dead money has an invisible cost
quiz.why: Opportunity cost never appears on a statement, but it's real; the clock frees the capital.

title: 39 · The money rules — sizing, caps, parcels and fees
steps: Size from risk, not conviction

The amateur question is 'how much do I want to buy?' The professional question is 'how much am I willing to LOSE if I'm wrong?' The 1%-risk rule (the dice icon in your rules) fixes that number — about 1% of the account per trade — and works backwards to the position size. (Your numbers and settings may differ — the mechanics are the lesson.)
The maths, drawn

Risk 1% of $50,000 = $500 at risk (not spent — AT RISK). If the 🛑 stop sits 8% below entry, then $500 ÷ 8% = $6,250 of shares. The 📦 10% position cap trims that to $5,000. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 128' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='12' y='14' width='60' height='18' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><text x='78' y='27' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='9' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>account $50,000</text><polygon points='42,32 42,40 38,40 44,48 50,40 46,40 46,32' fill='#f5c84c'/><rect x='12' y='50' width='22' height='18' rx='1.5' fill='#f5c84c'/><text x='40' y='63' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.6' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>1% of account = $500 AT RISK (not spent — at risk)</text><polygon points='23,68 23,76 19,76 25,84 31,76 27,76 27,68' fill='#60a5fa'/><rect x='12' y='86' width='150' height='18' rx='1.5' fill='#60a5fa'/><text x='168' y='99' fill='#60a5fa' font-size='8.6' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>÷ 8% stop gap → $6,250 raw size</text><rect x='12' y='110' width='120' height='14' rx='1.5' fill='#4ade80'/><text x='138' y='121' fill='#4ade80' font-size='8.6' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>📦 10% cap trims it → $5,000 final buy</text></svg>Notice what happened: a TIGHTER stop allows a BIGGER position for the same risk; a wider stop forces a smaller one. Risk stays constant; size breathes.
Why the 📦 cap exists at all

The 1% rule alone would happily put 40% of the account in one share with a tight stop — and stops can be jumped in a gap. The cap is the second seatbelt: no single name may own too much of your fate, whatever the risk maths says.
The $500 minimum parcel

Below a certain size, a trade can't pay for its own costs. A $3 brokerage fee on a $500 parcel is 0.6% on the way in and 0.6% on the way out — the share must rise over 1.2% just to reach zero. On a $5,000 parcel the same fee is a rounding error. Small parcels aren't cautious; they're expensive.
Fees and slippage — the honest ledger

The paper trader charges the brokerage YOU set on every buy and sell (set it in the portfolio settings to match your real broker; default 0 until you do) and can model slippage — fills happen at the NEXT day's open, like a real order queued overnight. The practice ledger is only worth keeping if it lies to you as little as possible.
🔢 The portfolio-level rules

Max open positions spreads the risk across enough names that no single story dominates; max buys per day stops one hot afternoon concentrating the account; and the cash check is absolute — the bot can never spend practice money it doesn't have.
One system, one sentence

Risk fixed at ~1%, size derived from the stop, capped by 📦, floored at $500, fees charged, positions and days capped. Boring on purpose — the excitement budget is spent on finding signals, never on sizing them.

quiz.q: With 1% risk on $50,000 and an 8% stop, the position is about…
quiz.why: $500 at risk ÷ 8% stop distance = $6,250 of shares. The at-risk dollars and the spent dollars are different numbers.

quiz.q: A TIGHTER stop, same 1% risk, means…
a: A bigger position — same dollars at risk over a shorter distance
quiz.why: Size breathes so risk can stay constant. (And the 📦 cap stands guard over the extreme cases.)

quiz.q: Why does the 📦 cap exist when the 1% rule already limits risk?
a: Stops can be gapped past — the cap stops any single name owning too much of your fate regardless of the maths
To make buys smaller for fees
quiz.why: Two independent seatbelts: one measures planned risk, the other limits concentration when plans fail.

quiz.q: Why refuse parcels under $500?
a: Fixed fees make tiny parcels expensive — a $3 fee each way on $500 needs >1.2% just to break even
quiz.why: Costs are a percentage tax that explodes as parcels shrink. Minimums keep the practice ledger honest.

title: 40 · 📏 New 52-week High — why 'too expensive' is a trap
steps: What the signal is

A share closes ABOVE the highest price it reached in the whole past year (250 trading days), with at least some extra volume behind it. Not 'near its high' — through it. The app measures the ceiling from the year ENDING YESTERDAY, so today's close is judged against a bar it didn't help set. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polyline points='12,72 40,64 66,74 94,58 122,66 150,52 178,60 206,46 232,54 258,42 282,48 306,26' fill='none' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='2.2'/><line x1='12' y1='38' x2='288' y2='38' stroke='#f5c84c' stroke-width='1.4' stroke-dasharray='5 4'/><text x='14' y='33' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>the past YEAR'S highest close — the ceiling</text><circle cx='306' cy='26' r='4' fill='#4ade80'/><text x='240' y='18' fill='#4ade80' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>today: CLOSED ABOVE IT</text><text x='14' y='96' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>a year of sellers said "no higher" — today the buyers won</text></svg>
Why it can work at all

It sounds backwards — surely you buy LOW? But a share at a yearly high has no trapped sellers waiting to 'get out even', and research has found people irrationally avoid buying near highs ('I've missed it'), so the move often has further to run. The feeling of 'too expensive' is the anchor talking, not the evidence. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='14' width='145' height='80' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#3a4a7a' stroke-width='1.2'/><rect x='165' y='14' width='145' height='80' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#3a4a7a' stroke-width='1.2'/><text x='18' y='28' fill='#f87171' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>WHAT IT FEELS LIKE</text><text x='18' y='46' fill='#e8eef7' font-size='9' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>"$5 → $8? I missed it."</text><text x='18' y='62' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>"It has to come back</text><text x='18' y='74' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>down… right?"</text><text x='173' y='28' fill='#4ade80' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>WHAT THE DATA SAYS</text><text x='173' y='46' fill='#e8eef7' font-size='9' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>no trapped sellers above</text><text x='173' y='62' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>everyone who owns it</text><text x='173' y='74' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>is already winning</text></svg>
How the app grades it — no free credibility

📏 New 52-week High sits on the 🧪 All-scans card like every signal: re-run over your stored year, followed forward 5, 10 and 20 days, measured against the whole market. It starts TOO EARLY and must earn SOLID before it means anything — and it needs 200+ stored days per share, so its numbers stay thin until your history runs deep. A famous signal gets judged exactly like an unknown one.

quiz.q: The 📏 signal fires when a share…
a: gets close to its yearly high
CLOSES ABOVE its highest close of the past year, on extra volume
rises three days in a row
quiz.why: Near the high is nothing — through it is the signal. The ceiling comes from the year ending yesterday, and volume has to back the move.

quiz.q: Why can buying at a yearly high work?
a: Nobody above is waiting to 'get out even', and people irrationally avoid buying near highs
quiz.why: No trapped sellers overhead, plus the well-documented 'I've missed it' anchor keeping buyers away longer than the evidence justifies.

quiz.q: How much trust does this famous signal start with on the report card?
a: TOO EARLY — it must earn its tier like everything else
quiz.why: Textbook fame counts for nothing here. It gets graded on your stored year and earns SOLID or it doesn't.

title: 41 · ✝️ Golden Cross — the slowest signal in the app
steps: Two averages, one crossing

Take the average close of the last 50 days (fast line) and the last 200 days (slow line). After a long decline the fast line sits BELOW the slow one. When a recovery is real and sustained, the fast line climbs up THROUGH the slow one — that crossing day, and only that day, is the Golden Cross. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polyline points='12,40 60,52 108,66 156,70 204,62 252,48 306,34' fill='none' stroke='#f5c84c' stroke-width='2'/><polyline points='12,30 60,40 108,50 156,58 204,60 252,58 306,54' fill='none' stroke='#7d95bd' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='6 3'/><circle cx='233' cy='55' r='5' fill='none' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='2'/><text x='200' y='90' fill='#4ade80' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>THE CROSS — one day only</text><text x='14' y='18' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>50-day average (fast)</text><text x='120' y='18' fill='#7d95bd' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>· · · 200-day average (slow)</text></svg>
Why one day only, and why so rare

The app fires ✝️ only on the day the fast average actually crosses the slow one — not every day it stays above (that would just duplicate 🧱 Strong Trends). A share does this maybe once or twice a year, so fires are RARE by design: expect small counts on the card and be patient before judging its tier. Slow signals aren't worse — they're answering a different question: 'has the whole trend changed?', not 'what moved today?'
The dark twin

The same maths runs in reverse: the fast average falling DOWN through the slow one is the 'death cross' — a classic warning that a long uptrend may be ending. The app doesn't act on it yet, but when the sell-side tools grow, this is the first warning light they'll get. A signal you understand in both directions is worth two you only half know.

quiz.q: The ✝️ Golden Cross fires…
a: every day the 50-day average is above the 200-day
only on the DAY the 50-day crosses up through the 200-day
quiz.why: The crossing day only. 'Is above' is a different, always-on condition — that's 🧱 Strong Trends' territory.

quiz.q: Why does the Golden Cross fire so rarely?
a: The app limits it to 10 a day
A share's 50/200 averages only cross once or twice a year — it marks a WHOLE trend changing
quiz.why: It's built from 250 days of prices, so it moves slowly and speaks seldom. Small fire counts on the card are expected, not broken.

quiz.q: The same maths running in reverse (fast average falling through slow) is called…
a: a death cross — a classic warning
quiz.why: The death cross is the mirror image: a long uptrend possibly ending. Understanding both directions makes the signal twice as useful.

title: 42 · 🌀 RSI Recovery — the bounce, not the fall
steps: RSI in one picture

RSI squeezes the last 14 days of gains-versus-losses into one number from 0 to 100. Persistent falling drags it toward 0; persistent rising pushes it toward 100. Below 30 the market calls a share 'oversold' — the selling has been relentless. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='24' width='296' height='52' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#3a4a7a' stroke-width='1.2'/><line x1='98' y1='24' x2='98' y2='76' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><line x1='218' y1='24' x2='218' y2='76' stroke='#f5c84c' stroke-width='1.2' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><text x='14' y='18' fill='#f87171' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>0</text><text x='92' y='18' fill='#f87171' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>30</text><text x='212' y='18' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>70</text><text x='296' y='18' fill='#4ade80' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>100</text><text x='24' y='54' fill='#f87171' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>OVERSOLD</text><text x='130' y='54' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='9' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>normal territory</text><text x='238' y='54' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>OVERHEATED</text><text x='14' y='92' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>RSI: fourteen days of tug-of-war, scored 0–100</text></svg>
The falling-knife trap

Here's what the textbooks gloss over: 'oversold' is NOT a buy signal. A collapsing share is oversold at 25, more oversold at 15, ruinously oversold at 8 — all the way down. Buying because RSI is low is catching a falling knife. The information isn't in being down there; it's in COMING BACK. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polyline points='12,20 50,34 88,48 126,62 164,76 190,84' fill='none' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='2.2'/><text x='30' y='16' fill='#f87171' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>RSI 25… 18… 11 — "oversold" the whole way down</text><polyline points='190,84 226,78 258,64 292,50' fill='none' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='2.2'/><circle cx='240' cy='73' r='5' fill='none' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='2'/><text x='196' y='97' fill='#4ade80' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>the signal: RSI crosses BACK UP through 30</text></svg>
What 🌀 actually tests, and where it fits

🌀 RSI Recovery fires only when yesterday's RSI was UNDER 30 and today's is 30 or higher — the first evidence the bounce has begun, never the hope that one might. It's the app's one true 'buy the recovery' signal, a counterweight to a roster that mostly chases strength (highs, streaks, leaders). Different engines fail at different times — that's why the 🧩 combinations table checks whether signals agree.

quiz.q: A share's RSI has been under 30 for two weeks. That alone means…
a: Nothing tradeable yet: shares can stay 'oversold' all the way down
quiz.why: Oversold is a description of the fall, not a prediction of the bounce. That's the falling-knife trap.

quiz.q: 🌀 fires when…
a: RSI crosses back UP through 30 — yesterday under, today at or above
quiz.why: The cross back up is the first measurable evidence the selling has exhausted. The signal is the recovery, not the wound.

quiz.q: Why is a mean-reversion signal useful in a momentum-heavy roster?
a: Different engines fail at different times — it works when chasing strength doesn't
quiz.why: Momentum signals starve in choppy markets; recovery signals starve in trending ones. A mixed roster means the card can show which engine suits the current weather.

title: 43 · 🤏 Volatility Squeeze — the coiled spring
steps: Quiet is information

Most signals hunt for something LOUD — a surge, a streak, a breakout. The squeeze hunts for the opposite: a share whose recent trading has narrowed to the TIGHTEST range it has managed in months, on drying-up volume. Markets alternate between rest and violence; an unusually deep rest often precedes an unusually big move. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><polyline points='12,30 30,74 48,26 66,70 84,32 102,66 120,38 138,62 156,44 174,58 192,48 210,55 228,50 246,54 264,51 282,53 306,52' fill='none' stroke='#7dd4ff' stroke-width='2'/><text x='14' y='16' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>wild ……………………………→ quieter ……→ dead still</text><rect x='222' y='42' width='88' height='18' rx='4' fill='none' stroke='#f5c84c' stroke-width='1.4' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><text x='226' y='78' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>its tightest stretch in months</text><text x='14' y='96' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>the spring is coiled — energy stored, direction unknown</text></svg>
The exact test — both halves matter

Two conditions, both required: the range must be the tightest it has been in months (not merely 'quiet-ish' — the app compares it against every comparable stretch in that period), AND volume must be BELOW normal. Quiet price on quiet volume means sellers have given up but buyers haven't arrived — genuine equilibrium. Quiet price on HEAVY volume is a different animal (that's 💎 accumulation territory), so the squeeze deliberately excludes it.
The honest limitation

A coiled spring stores energy — it doesn't choose a direction. Squeezes resolve down as often as up in theory; whether YOURS resolve up on your market is precisely what the 🧪 card will measure. This is the newcomer most likely to surprise us either way, which is exactly why it was worth adding: the card gets to answer a question the textbooks argue about.

quiz.q: 🤏 fires when the last 10 days are…
a: the TIGHTEST range in about 3 months, on below-normal volume
quiz.why: Deep rest, measured against every 10-day window of the past ~3 months — and the volume has to be drying up too.

quiz.q: Quiet price on HEAVY volume is excluded because…
a: it's a different signal — quiet accumulation — not a market at rest
quiz.why: The squeeze wants genuine equilibrium: sellers done, buyers not yet arrived. Heavy-volume quiet is somebody quietly buying — 💎's job.

quiz.q: What does a squeeze NOT tell you?
a: That the range is unusually tight
Which DIRECTION the eventual move will go
quiz.why: The spring stores energy without choosing a direction. Whether squeezes on your market resolve upward is what the report card exists to measure.

title: 44 · 🏁 Relative-Strength Leader — beating the market, not just rising
steps: Relative is the word that matters

A share up 8% in six months sounds fine — until you notice the whole market rose 20%. It didn't lead; it lagged. 🏁 ranks every share by how far it has run over recent months and keeps only the strongest slice OF THE WHOLE MARKET — a bar that moves every single day, set by everyone else's performance. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='14' width='300' height='80' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#3a4a7a' stroke-width='1.2'/><rect x='18' y='58' width='40' height='28' rx='2' fill='#54627f'/><text x='38' y='54' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>+3%</text><rect x='66' y='50' width='40' height='36' rx='2' fill='#54627f'/><text x='86' y='46' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>+8%</text><rect x='114' y='44' width='40' height='42' rx='2' fill='#54627f'/><text x='134' y='40' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>+14%</text><rect x='162' y='36' width='40' height='50' rx='2' fill='#54627f'/><text x='182' y='32' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>+21%</text><rect x='210' y='30' width='40' height='56' rx='2' fill='#54627f'/><text x='230' y='26' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>+29%</text><rect x='258' y='20' width='40' height='66' rx='2' fill='#f5c84c'/><text x='278' y='16' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8' font-weight='800' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>TOP 10%</text><text x='14' y='92' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'></text></svg>
Why this needed YOUR data

Most tools can't compute this honestly because ranking a share against the whole market requires holding the WHOLE market's history — every share, every day. Your pantry downloads exactly that, nightly. Each day of the replay, the app computes that day's cut-off across every share trading, then asks who cleared it. The bar is real, contemporary, and market-wide — not a guess or a fixed threshold.
Leaders on a breather, not on a spike

One more filter: the share must NOT be having a big day (today between −6% and +2%). Chasing a leader mid-spike buys the excitement at its most expensive; catching it flat or resting buys the same leadership without the froth. And a safety rail worth knowing: if the day's market-wide cut-off can't be computed, 🏁 refuses to fire at all — no bar, no signal, never a guess.

quiz.q: A share rose 8% in six months while the market rose 20%. Is it a leader?
a: No — it LAGGED the market by 12%
quiz.why: Leadership is relative. Absolute gains flatter everything in a rising market; the top-10% bar strips that flattery away.

quiz.q: Why can this app compute true relative strength when many tools can't?
a: It holds the WHOLE market's history nightly, so each day's top-10% cut-off is computed across everyone
quiz.why: The nightly pantry stores every share. The cut-off is recomputed per day from the entire market — a moving, honest bar.

quiz.q: Why must the share NOT be spiking today (−6% to +2%)?
a: Buying a leader mid-spike pays the froth; catching it on a breather buys the same leadership cheaper
It must be falling to qualify
quiz.why: The leadership was earned over 120 days; today's excitement isn't the edge, it's the cost. The signal waits for the breather.

title: 45 · 📰 News + Volume — the first signal built on facts
steps: An estimate grows up

Since the beginning, the app's 'news?' column has been an educated GUESS from price and volume footprints. Now your data server collects real headlines for the shares you care about — filtered so they're actually ABOUT the company, and graded for materiality: results, halts, takeovers and project approvals count; listicles and 'shares to watch' chatter are binned. 📰 News + Volume fires only when a CONFIRMED material headline lands on a day the share also traded unusually heavy volume — the news said something, and the market audibly reacted. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='10' y='14' width='143' height='36' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#3a4a7a' stroke-width='1.2'/><text x='18' y='28' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>1 · CONFIRMED headline</text><text x='18' y='42' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>results · halt · takeover…</text><rect x='167' y='14' width='143' height='36' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#3a4a7a' stroke-width='1.2'/><text x='175' y='28' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>2 · VOLUME 2× normal</text><text x='175' y='42' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='start' font-family='sans-serif'>the market reacted, loudly</text><rect x='88' y='62' width='143' height='30' rx='6' fill='none' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='160' y='81' fill='#4ade80' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>BOTH on the same day → 📰 fires</text></svg>
Fail-closed: the most honest signal in the app

Headlines are only collected for your shortlist — holdings, starred shares and each day's picks — so most of the market has NO coverage. Where there's no coverage, 📰 doesn't guess: it simply never fires. A missing signal is honest; a fabricated one is not. Expect tiny fire counts for months while coverage grows share by share. You can read the actual headlines any time: open any share's 🔬 detail panel and its 📰 Confirmed news section shows them, dated and labelled.
Why nobody else at this price has it

Signal products either ignore news or bolt on expensive feeds. Yours grew its own: the server fetches from public feeds, throws out anything that doesn't name the company, grades what remains, and stores it — automatically, for the shares you actually watch. Even so, the rule earns trust like every other: the 🧪 card grades it from birth, TOO EARLY until the fires accumulate. Facts about inputs, evidence about outcomes — both halves matter.

quiz.q: 📰 fires when…
a: a CONFIRMED material headline lands the same day volume runs at least 2× normal
volume is high three days running
quiz.why: Both halves: real, material, about-the-company news AND an audible market reaction, on the same day.

quiz.q: A share has no news coverage yet. What does 📰 do?
a: Falls back to the price-based estimate
Never fires for that share — a missing signal beats a fabricated one
quiz.why: Fail-closed. Where the facts run out, this signal stops — it never quietly swaps facts for guesses.

quiz.q: Where can you READ a share's confirmed headlines?
a: Only on the server admin pages
In the share's 🔬 detail panel — the 📰 Confirmed news section
quiz.why: Open any share's detail panel: dated headlines, kind labels, gold badges on the material ones, each linking to its source.

title: 46 · ⚖️ Evidence on the radar — how much a signal has proved
steps: A tier is a count, not a compliment

The 🧪 All-scans report card has always graded every signal by replaying a year of your own stored history. Those grades now come out of the card and onto the radar itself. SOLID means the signal fired 200+ times in that replayed year. PROMISING means 50+. TOO EARLY means under 50, where plain luck can still explain the whole record. Read that again, because it is the part people get wrong: a tier describes how many times we have seen it happen — it is a statement about sample size, not about how good the signal is or how much money it made. A six-fire signal showing +23% ranks below a five-hundred-fire signal showing +2%, because six fires is a story and five hundred is evidence.
Three tiles, tap any combination

The 🧪 Evidence group sits second in the Market Radar, so it is visible on a phone without unfolding anything. Each share is counted once, in the tile matching the strongest signal firing on it today — so the three numbers never double-count. You will almost always see a big SOLID number and zeros beside it, and that surprises everyone. Here is why, and it is worth understanding: a tier belongs to a signal, but these tiles count shares — and those are linked by the very thing the tier measures. A signal earns SOLID by firing hundreds of times; firing hundreds of times is exactly what makes it tag hundreds of shares. A signal is TOO EARLY because it has barely fired; barely firing means it tags almost nobody. So the share-tiles lean to SOLID by construction. The line underneath shows the distribution you were probably expecting — your signals themselves, sorted by record — and that one is genuinely lopsided the other way: on a typical market, several of the app's signals have not fired once all year. Tap 🟢 SOLID to cut the day's list down to shares a proven signal put there. Tap two tiles to see both groups together. Tap Showing to clear. Some days 🟢 SOLID shows nothing at all: that is the app being honest, not broken. "Do nothing today" is a real answer, and a tool that can never say it is a tool that is always selling you something.
The ⚖️ chip on the row, and what it lists

In 🏆 Top 20 and 🧩 All Signals each share also wears an ⚖️ chip — ⚖️ SOLID ×2 means two separate SOLID-graded signals are firing on it right now. Hold the chip (or hover) and the tooltip names every one of them with its tier and its fire count, so you can see exactly what earned the label. This is the whole philosophy in one chip: the app does not just tell you a share looks interesting, it tells you how much reason it has to think so — including when the answer is "not much".

quiz.q: A signal is graded SOLID. What does that tell you?
a: It has fired 200+ times in the replayed year — a big enough sample to lean on
quiz.why: Tiers measure sample size. SOLID = 200+ fires, PROMISING = 50+, TOO EARLY = under 50. It says how much evidence exists, not how good the result was.

quiz.q: Signal A: 6 fires, +23% average. Signal B: 500 fires, +2%. Which ranks higher?
a: B — six fires is a story, five hundred is evidence
quiz.why: Six fires can't be told apart from luck. The app deliberately demotes thin samples no matter how spectacular the numbers look.

quiz.q: You tap 🟢 SOLID and the table goes empty. What happened?
a: The app is broken — reload it
Nothing a proven signal flagged today. An honest 'no strong evidence', which is a real answer
quiz.why: Empty is a legitimate result. Check the line under the tiles though — if it says shares were 'not checked', that's a different situation (lesson 47).

quiz.q: ⚖️ SOLID ×3 on a row means…
a: The share went up three days
Three separate SOLID-graded signals are firing on it today
quiz.why: The ×N counts how many SOLID-graded signals fired. Hold the chip to see each one named with its tier and fire count.

title: 47 · 💧 Why a share shows no tier — checked, or never tested?
steps: A true story: the share that vanished

Carnaby Resources closed +57% on 25 million shares against an 885,000 average, above its 200-day line, flagged Breakout and Volume Record. The Evidence tiles read 0 / 0 / 0. It should have read ⚖️ SOLID ×6. The cause was not the grading — it was a gate that fires before any signal is tested. The 🧪 card has a 💧 floor: skip shares whose daily turnover is so small that their "returns" are mostly bid-ask noise. Sensible. But that floor measures the share's three-month average turnover, and Carnaby's average was $668k — under a $1m floor. So it was dropped before a single rule ran.
Absence of evidence vs absence of a test

Here is the bit worth carrying with you, in the app and out of it. "We looked and found nothing" and "we never looked" are completely different claims, and they used to render identically as a zero. From this version the app tells you which one it is: under the Evidence tiles you may now see 💧 4 not checked — below your $1m floor, or 📉 2 need more history, and the share's own row wears a grey 💧 not checked chip instead of a blank. A blank space that means two different things is worse than no information at all, because it quietly invites you to read it as the reassuring one. That principle then decided how this ends. Once the app could SAY how many shares it was skipping, the number turned out to be enormous — on a normal day 173 of 227 — so from v462 the daily check simply includes every share. A thin share is now tested and counted like any other; it just wears a 💧 on its ⚖️ chip to say it may be hard to trade. Hiding a share told you less than warning you does.
Where the floor lives, and the trap in it

The floor is the 💧 row on the 🧪 All-scans report card: Any · $50k · $250k · $1m · $5m. The trap: on first run it inherits the app's own 💧 filter, so if you screen for liquid names you have set your grading floor too, without ever opening the card. If a share you care about reads "not checked", lower the floor and it gets tested. The floor did not go away — it moved to where it belongs. It still decides what the year-long grading replay measures (a tier describes a year of behaviour, and a share must have been tradeable across that year for its record to mean anything — one spike does not make a year) and what the 🤖 auto-pilot may buy (it must never buy something it cannot get out of). What it no longer does is decide what you are allowed to see. One setting had been answering three different questions; now each gets the answer it deserves.

quiz.q: The Evidence tiles read 0 / 0 / 0 and the line below says '💧 4 not checked'. What do you know?
a: Four shares were tested and failed
Four shares were never tested — they sit below your 💧 grading floor
quiz.why: Not checked means no signal was tested on them. That's a missing test, not a verdict. Lower the floor on the 🧪 card to include them.

quiz.q: The 💧 grading floor measures a share's turnover using…
quiz.why: The average — because a tier describes a year of behaviour, and one big day doesn't make a share consistently tradeable.

quiz.q: The $1M+ Traded tile lights up for a share, but the evidence check skipped it. Is something broken?
a: No — the tile measures TODAY's turnover, the floor measures the three-month AVERAGE
quiz.why: Two different quantities wearing the same dollar sign. A share that just woke up can clear today's bar and still sit under its average-based floor.

quiz.q: Where did your 💧 grading floor come from if you never set it?
a: On first run it inherits the app's own 💧 filter
quiz.why: Screening for liquid names silently sets the grading floor too. Worth checking on the 🧪 card if shares are being skipped.

quiz.q: Why does the app bother distinguishing 'not checked' from zero?
a: Because 'we looked and found nothing' and 'we never looked' are different claims, and only one of them is what a zero implies
quiz.why: The tiles promise an honest zero. That promise is only kept for shares actually tested — so the app has to say when one wasn't.

title: 48 · 💵 Value traded — the tiles that ask 'could I get out?'
steps: Volume counts shares. Value counts money.

Two new tiles sit at the end of the Volume group: $250k+ Traded and $1M+ Traded. They count shares where today's close × today's volume clears that much value, in the exchange's own currency. Why add them when there is already a volume column? Because volume alone lies to you about size. Two million shares of a one-cent stock is twenty thousand dollars — a market you can move by yourself. Twenty thousand shares of a hundred-dollar stock is over two million dollars. The bigger volume is the smaller market.
What the tiles are really asking

The honest question behind them is not "is this exciting?" but "if I buy this and change my mind, can I get out without wearing the spread?" In a thin market your own order moves the price against you both ways — buying in and selling out. That is a cost that never appears in any signal's return figure. Tap a tile to filter to those shares, tap it again to clear, and it stacks with everything else on the radar. Missing price or volume gives no answer, so those shares are excluded rather than assumed good.
The disagreement you will eventually notice

These tiles measure today. The 💧 evidence floor (lesson 47) measures the three-month average. So a share that just woke up can light $1M+ Traded and still be skipped by the evidence check — two different quantities wearing the same dollar sign. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. "Could I trade this today?" is a question about today. "Has this share been tradeable long enough for a year of history to mean anything?" is a question about the year. Now you know which is which, and the app will tell you when they disagree.

quiz.q: Which represents the bigger market?
a: The one with more shares, always
quiz.why: $20,000 vs $2,240,000. Share count alone tells you almost nothing about how much money is really changing hands.

quiz.q: The turnover tiles are calculated from…
quiz.why: Today's close × today's volume, in the exchange's own currency — a snapshot of today's tradeability.

quiz.q: Why does thin turnover matter even if a signal looks great?
a: Your own order moves the price against you going in and coming out — a cost no return figure shows
quiz.why: The spread is a real cost that never appears in a backtest's return. That's also why the grading has a floor at all.

quiz.q: A share lights $1M+ Traded but the evidence check skipped it. Why?
a: The tile measures today; the evidence floor measures the three-month average
quiz.why: Different questions: can I trade it today, versus has it been tradeable long enough for a year of record to mean anything.

title: 49 · 🔬 The six newer signals, in plain English
steps: Six different ways of asking the same question

Every signal in this app is asking one question — is something happening to this share that usually isn't? — and each of the six newer ones asks it differently. Here they are with the jargon taken out. Lessons 40 to 45 go into each one properly; this is the map you read first. Since 2026 they also have their own 🔬 Signals row on the Market Radar, so you can see how many shares are firing each one today and tap to filter to them.
📏 New 52-week High — "nobody who owns it is losing money"

It closed higher than it has closed on any day in the past year. Think about what that means for the people holding it: every single one of them is in profit. Nobody is sitting there waiting to sell the moment it gets back to what they paid. That waiting crowd is what usually caps a rising price, and here there isn't one. It sounds backwards — the share is at its most expensive, and that's the good news — which is exactly why most people ignore it.
✝️ Golden Cross — "the slow average finally caught up"

Take the average price over the last 50 days, and the average over the last 200 days. When the 50 rises above the 200, that's a golden cross. Averages are slow and boring on purpose: a single wild day barely moves them, so when they cross it's because the trend genuinely changed, not because of one exciting Tuesday. It's slow to show up and slow to go away. There's a dark twin called a death cross (50 falling below 200) which the app warns you about on shares you own.
🌀 RSI Recovery — "it stopped falling and started climbing"

RSI is a 0-to-100 measure of how hard a share has been pushed lately. Under 30 means it's been beaten up. Now here's the trap: cheap can always get cheaper, and "it's oversold!" has emptied a lot of wallets. So this signal doesn't fire when a share is beaten up. It fires when a beaten-up share climbs back out — RSI crossing back up through 30. The turn is the signal, not the fall.
🤏 Volatility Squeeze — "it's gone very quiet"

This one has no opinion about direction, and that honesty is the point. It fires when the share's daily range is the tightest it has been in about three months, on light volume. Like a spring being wound: the quiet usually ends in a move. But it might be a move down. Anyone who tells you a squeeze predicts which way is selling you something. Treat it as "watch this one", never as "buy this one".
🏁 Rel-Strength Leader — "beating the market, not just going up"

In a market where everything is rising, going up proves nothing — you'd have done as well throwing a dart. This signal marks the shares in the strongest slice of the entire market by how much they've gained over the past 120 days, caught while taking a breather rather than mid-sprint. It's the difference between a fast runner and a runner on a moving walkway.
📰 News + Volume — "real news, and the crowd reacted"

Every other signal in the app is an estimate from price and volume. This one needs a fact: a confirmed, material headline — results, a takeover, a trading halt, a big approval — landing on a day the share also traded unusually heavy volume. Something real was said, and the market audibly reacted to it. And when there's no news coverage for a share, it doesn't guess: it simply never fires. A missing signal is honest; an invented one isn't.
The bit that matters more than any of the six

A signal tells you where to look. It does not tell you whether looking there has ever paid off — that's a completely different question, and the 🧪 All-scans report card answers it by replaying the whole year. All six of these are new, which means most of them are still marked TOO EARLY: fired too few times for anyone, including us, to know if they work. That label isn't us being modest, it's us refusing to pretend. When you see one fire, the right thought is "interesting, what else is going on with this share?" — never "the app said buy". It didn't, and it won't.

quiz.q: Why is a new 52-week high a good thing rather than 'too expensive'?
a: Because everyone holding it is in profit, so nobody is waiting to sell just to break even
Because it must be a big company
quiz.why: No trapped sellers overhead. That waiting crowd is what usually caps a rising price, and at a new high there isn't one.

quiz.q: 🌀 RSI Recovery fires when…
a: A beaten-up share climbs back UP through 30
quiz.why: The turn is the signal, not the fall. Cheap can always get cheaper — 'it's oversold' has emptied a lot of wallets.

quiz.q: 🤏 A Volatility Squeeze tells you a move is coming. Which way?
a: Up — that's the point of it
Nobody knows. It's a coiled spring with no direction
quiz.why: It has no opinion about direction, and saying so is the honest part. Anyone claiming a squeeze predicts direction is selling you something.

quiz.q: Why does 🏁 Rel-Strength compare a share to the whole market?
a: Because in a rising market going up proves nothing — beating everyone else does
quiz.why: A fast runner versus a runner on a moving walkway. Rising with the tide isn't skill; outpacing it might be.

quiz.q: A share has no news coverage. What does 📰 News + Volume do?
a: Never fires for it — a missing signal beats an invented one
quiz.why: Fail-closed. Where the facts run out, this signal stops rather than quietly swapping facts for guesses.

quiz.q: Most of the six are marked TOO EARLY. What should you do with them?
a: Use them to decide where to LOOK, while the report card works out whether looking there pays off
Trust them — new signals are the best ones
quiz.why: TOO EARLY means fired too few times for anyone to know yet. They point you somewhere; they don't tell you it's a good place.

title: 50 · SOLID & PROMISING — the two bars, drawn
steps: Two questions decide every badge

Every tier on the 📋 report card — SOLID, PROMISING, or not proven — comes from just two questions asked of each signal line. 1: Has it had enough tries? One lucky win proves nothing. 2: Is the edge real, or just luck bouncing around? Both must be answered well; a huge edge from 12 fires fails question 1, and 500 fires with a wobbly edge fail question 2. Nothing else — not how exciting the flag sounds, not how big its best week was — moves the badge.
First, every fire is scored fairly

Before either question, each fire gets an honest score: how the share moved over the next days minus how the AVERAGE share moved those same days. That subtraction matters — in a roaring market every flag looks clever, so a fire only earns credit for beating the market it lived in. Extreme moves are capped at ±35% so one moonshot can't buy a badge, and only shares liquid enough to actually trade (about $50k+/day) are counted at all — an edge you couldn't have bought isn't an edge.
Question 1 — enough tries

The fire count over the graded year. 30+ fires reaches the PROMISING bar; 50+ fires reaches the SOLID bar. Below 30, the app says TOO EARLY — which is honest, not harsh: it simply hasn't seen enough to know. Rare combos live here for a long time, and that's fine.
Question 2 — strength: real or luck?

The strength number compares the average edge to how wildly the results swing. Both lines above average positive — but the top one is noise wearing a costume, and the bottom one is a real pattern. Strength 1.0 means the edge is as big as its own noise (the PROMISING bar); strength 2.0 means it's twice as big — roughly a few-in-a-hundred chance of being pure luck (the SOLID bar). One important detail: strength is measured across DAYS, not across individual fires. Two hundred shares firing the same flag on one morning is one piece of evidence about that morning, not two hundred — they all rise and fall together. Counting them as two hundred would make almost anything look certain, so the app averages each day first and then asks how consistent the days were.
The ladder, all together

Put the two questions side by side and you get the ladder every line climbs: A line can be stuck for two different reasons — not enough fires (just needs time) or fires but no strength (may never make it). The 🌱 nursery on the card tells you which bar each climber still has to clear, and which way it's trending.
🏛 The crown — held across all three years

Since the server learned three years of history, there's one badge above SOLID: the line's edge shows in the CURRENT year (that's what decides its tier — an edge that died in an old year can never hide inside a three-year average), and it earned a ✓ in both earlier years separately (right direction and strength ≥1 in each). The card writes it as 🏛 held across all three years. It is the strongest evidence this app can offer — and still never a guarantee: the honest reading of every badge is “this DID work”, never “this WILL work”.

title: 51 — The Paula–Niño Edge: money on a $0-to-$3.50 scale
steps: Edge is dollars, not a mystery number

When the card says a signal has an edge of +2.42%, it means: put $100 into the share the day after the signal appears, wait the outcome window, and on average you end up about $2.42 AHEAD OF THE MARKET — beyond what the average share did, before brokerage. Put in $1,000, it's about $24. The card now writes it that way: +$2.42 per $100.
The scale — what's high and what's low

The realistic range for end-of-day price signals is $0 to about $3.50 per $100. Under $0.50: real but too small — trading costs usually eat it. $0.50–$2: decent. $2–$3.50: strong — as good as this kind of signal gets. The little bar next to every edge is filled against that FIXED scale, so a full-ish green bar means the same thing on every card, every day.
Too good = broken, not jackpot

Anything above about $3.50 per $100, repeated over hundreds of sightings, is a red flag — a data error, a few freak trades dragging the average, or an edge so obvious the market would erase it instantly. The app paints those RED and says 'check this'. Excitement is the wrong response to a huge edge; suspicion is the right one.
Why edges are small and get smaller

An edge is money lying on the table. The bigger and easier it is to see, the faster other traders pile in — buying earlier and earlier until the gap closes. That's why $2–$3 is the top of the realistic scale, and why an edge that PERSISTS across years (the ✓ marks) is worth more than a bigger one that just appeared. One more thing: this number carries a name — the Paula–Niño Edge, PN Edge for short — named in memory of Paula and Niño. It is the most honest number in this app: it never promises, it only reports what was measured. That is a good thing to put a loved name on.

title: 52 — Windows: the app's three kinds of time
steps: Trading days, not calendar days
Every number in this app counts days the market was open. 5 trading days = one real week. 30 trading days = about six weeks. 250 trading days = about one year. Weekends and holidays never count.
The outcome window — how long a signal gets to prove itself

When a signal appears on a share, the app pretends to buy at the NEXT day's close (you only see an end-of-day signal after the market shuts) and then measures the move over the next week (5d) or six weeks (30d). That stretch is the outcome window. The switch on the report card changes it — and changes the question: 'does this pop within a week?' vs 'does this play out over six weeks?' The same signal can pass one and fail the other.
The graded year and the pantry

'Seen 1,503 times' counts sightings across the most recent YEAR of data (250 trading days), on every tradeable share at once. Behind that sits the pantry: three years of stored history, which is what lets the app also grade the two OLDER years separately — the ✓/✗ era marks — and ask whether an edge has lasted.
One ruler at a time

Numbers from different windows must never be compared — a $0.40 edge over one week and a $1.20 edge over six weeks might be the same signal on different rulers. The app enforces this: era marks and trajectories only light up when they were graded on the SAME window you're viewing.

title: 53 — Badges: the good news and the bad news
steps: What a badge literally is

A badge is a grade on PAST homework. The app re-marks a signal over the last year and asks two things: did it appear often enough to judge (30+ sightings for BUILDING/PROMISING, 50+ for PROVEN/SOLID), and did it beat the market by more than luck could explain? Clear both bars, badge. Nothing about tomorrow is in it.
The good news

A badge means 'not a fluke'. Hundreds of sightings, measured against the market, strong enough to stand clear of noise. Without badges you'd be trading on vibes — and the whole point of this app is that vibes lie. A badge is the difference between a pattern you BELIEVE in and one that's been COUNTED.
The bad news

A badge is always about the past — and by the time a pattern has proven itself 50 times, some of its magic may be spent. The app's own self-test measured this: on average, about 71% of a badge's edge faded in the year AFTER it was earned. A badge can be a certificate handed out at the after-party.
How to hold both truths

Never read a badge alone. Read it as a sentence with its neighbours: the ✓/✗ era marks (did it work in earlier years too?) and the trajectory arrow (growing or fading?). PROVEN + ✓✓ + ↗ is the strongest thing this app can say. PROVEN + ✗✗ + ↘ means 'aced last year's exam, failing this year's' — a badge to walk past.

title: 54 — The self-test: does grading arrive too late?
steps: The fear, stated plainly

'By the time the app has proven a signal, the good times are over — we'll buy the top.' That's the sharpest objection anyone can raise against evidence-first trading, and the ⚖ report answers it with your own data instead of a sales pitch.
How the test works — the tipster check

You can't judge a footy tipster on this week's tips; the games haven't been played. You dig up LAST season's tips and check them against results he couldn't have known. Same here: the app rewinds to an earlier year, notes which signals held a badge right then, and scores them ONLY on the year that followed. The badge never gets to peek at its own exam.
What it found on this market

Pooled across all badges: +$0.27 per $100 when earned, +$0.08 in the year after — a 71% fade. BUT the fade wasn't even. Team-ups (two or three signals agreeing on the same share, the same day — like Breakout + big-money buying) KEPT their edge and some grew. Loners (one signal alone) went negative. The fade is almost entirely the loners' fault.
What to do with that

Treat badges on single signals as history lessons. Treat badges on team-ups — especially the Breakout + Big money? family — as the one thing this data has properly earned your attention. That's why 🎯 Best Evidence Today ranks team-ups first: it isn't taste, it's the exam result. And re-run the ⚖ self-test after every re-grade — if the answer ever changes, the app will say so.

title: 55 · Five ways a backtest flatters itself
steps: Why this lesson exists

Every number in this app came out of a test. Tests can be wrong in ways that make results look BETTER than they were — and the wrongness never announces itself. This lesson lists the five faults we have actually found in our own testing, what each one did to the numbers, and how to spot it. Nothing here is hypothetical: every one of these was caught in this app's own results, and two of them changed headline figures the lessons used to teach.
Fault 1 — the test knew the future

The big one. To decide whether a share was worth buying on a Tuesday in 2021, the test used a signal score computed from ALL the history — including everything that happened after that Tuesday. It only picked signals that turned out to work, then measured how well those picks did. Of course they did well; the answer was baked in. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 104' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='14' y1='52' x2='306' y2='52' stroke='#3a4a7a' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='120' cy='52' r='7' fill='#f5c84c'/><text x='120' y='40' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>the buy</text><path d='M 270 74 Q 195 92 128 62' fill='none' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='1.8' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><polygon points='128,58 122,66 134,66' fill='#f87171'/><text x='196' y='102' fill='#f87171' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>the score was built from THIS</text><text x='276' y='46' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>the future</text><text x='50' y='46' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>the past</text><text x='160' y='16' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>a buy decision that quietly borrowed tomorrow's newspaper</text></svg>Fixed by grading in rolling windows — each stretch scored only on what came before it. The correction was brutal: the headline win rate fell from about half the trades winning to about a third.
What look-ahead does NOT ruin

Worth being precise, because the fix is not 'throw everything away'. Look-ahead inflates the ABSOLUTE numbers — the return, the win rate. It affects every rule set roughly equally, so COMPARISONS between them mostly survive: a trailing exit still beat a fixed take-profit by a wide margin under both methods. Trust the ranking; distrust the size. That is the general shape of this whole lesson.
Fault 2 — one coin flip is not a benchmark

To prove picks beat luck you compare them against random picks. But ONE set of random picks can land anywhere — brilliant or terrible — by chance. We once ran a single random comparison and it beat the strategy; ran properly as 200 separate random runs, the same strategy sat above the 95th percentile of them. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 100' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='14' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>200 random runs — a whole spread, not one answer</text><rect x='30' y='68' width='12' height='10' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='48' y='60' width='12' height='18' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='66' y='48' width='12' height='30' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='84' y='38' width='12' height='40' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='102' y='32' width='12' height='46' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='120' y='36' width='12' height='42' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='138' y='44' width='12' height='34' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='156' y='54' width='12' height='24' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='174' y='62' width='12' height='16' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><rect x='192' y='70' width='12' height='8' rx='1.5' fill='#54627f'/><line x1='262' y1='24' x2='262' y2='78' stroke='#4ade80' stroke-width='2.4'/><text x='262' y='20' fill='#4ade80' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>the strategy</text><line x1='14' y1='78' x2='306' y2='78' stroke='#3a4a7a' stroke-width='1'/><text x='108' y='94' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>most random runs land in here</text><text x='262' y='94' fill='#4ade80' font-size='8' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>above 95% of them</text></svg>A single random run is an anecdote. Ask how many were run, and where the strategy sat in the spread.
Fault 3 — the slippage ladder tests different books

A stress test raises the assumed trading cost — 0.5%, 1%, 1.5%, 2% — to see where the edge dies. It reads as one strategy getting more expensive. It isn't. A different cost changes each fill price, which changes how many shares you can afford, which changes when a position slot frees up, which changes WHICH SHARES YOU END UP OWNING. The tell is easy to spot: if a HIGHER cost ever produces a HIGHER return, the rungs are not the same book — and we have seen exactly that. Read the ladder as four related experiments, never as one dial.
Fault 4 — measuring concentration in the wrong unit

The honest question is 'how much of the profit came from a couple of lucky trades?' We were answering it by adding up the top three trades' PERCENTAGE returns, which cannot answer it: a +400% gain on a tiny early parcel and a +40% gain on a large late one are wildly different amounts of money and the percentages say the opposite. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 96' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='24' y='26' width='36' height='18' rx='2' fill='#f5c84c'/><text x='42' y='20' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>+400%</text><text x='42' y='58' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='7.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>on a small parcel</text><text x='42' y='72' fill='#4ade80' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>$800</text><rect x='196' y='26' width='84' height='18' rx='2' fill='#60a5fa'/><text x='238' y='20' fill='#60a5fa' font-size='8.5' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>+40%</text><text x='238' y='58' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='7.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>on a large parcel</text><text x='238' y='72' fill='#4ade80' font-size='9' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>$4,000</text><text x='160' y='92' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>the bigger PERCENTAGE made one fifth of the money</text></svg>The fix is one line: report the profit WITHOUT the top three trades, in dollars. It reads the same whether the account won or lost, and it is the number the question was always about.
Fault 5 — every company in the test survived

The stored history holds the shares that exist TODAY, ten years back. Companies that were suspended, taken over or wound up in those ten years were never asked for, so they are not in the data at all. Every year the ASX loses well over a hundred listings, and for shares under a dollar the usual ending is suspension and removal. <svg viewBox='0 0 320 92' style='max-width:340px;width:100%;display:block;margin:8px 0' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><text x='160' y='14' fill='#8fa0c9' font-size='8.5' font-weight='400' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>ten years of a real market</text><circle cx='40' cy='42' r='8' fill='#4ade80' opacity='.7'/><circle cx='72' cy='42' r='8' fill='#4ade80' opacity='.7'/><circle cx='104' cy='42' r='8' fill='#4ade80' opacity='.7'/><circle cx='136' cy='42' r='8' fill='#4ade80' opacity='.7'/><circle cx='168' cy='42' r='8' fill='#f87171' opacity='.55'/><circle cx='200' cy='42' r='8' fill='#f87171' opacity='.55'/><circle cx='232' cy='42' r='8' fill='#f87171' opacity='.55'/><circle cx='264' cy='42' r='8' fill='#f87171' opacity='.55'/><line x1='158' y1='30' x2='274' y2='54' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='1.4'/><text x='88' y='68' fill='#4ade80' font-size='8' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>still listed — IN the test</text><text x='216' y='68' fill='#f87171' font-size='8' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>gone — MISSING entirely</text><text x='160' y='86' fill='#f5c84c' font-size='8' font-weight='700' text-anchor='middle' font-family='sans-serif'>the test cannot lose money on a company that failed</text></svg>This one cannot be fixed by any setting, so it must be labelled instead: every long-window figure in this app is an UPPER BOUND. Treat it as the best case, not the expected case.
The cost line — an edge smaller than the brokerage is not an edge

Not a fault in the test, but the most common misreading of a good one. A round trip on a $500 parcel is roughly 1.2% of it. So a signal with an average edge of +0.30% is not a small winner — it is a loser once the broker is paid. When we applied this to a ten-year grading, HALF the signals on the honour roll fell below the line. Always ask of any edge: does it clear the round trip? If not, it belongs in the research pile, not the buy list. And these tests have already earned their keep once: the dip entry sat at 5% for years, and the ten-year ladder showed the deeper limit was MISSING winners rather than filtering losers — so it moved to 2%, the first shipped setting these five corrections changed.
What survived all five

This is not a lesson about nothing working. After every correction above, the same three findings held: a trailing exit beat a fixed take-profit by a wide margin; the sub-$1 band beat the rest of the market; and picks chosen on graded evidence beat properly-run random picks. What did NOT survive was the SIZE of every one of those claims. The direction of our evidence has been robust. The magnitude has been optimistic every single time.
The habit to take away

When any test — ours or anyone's — shows you a result, ask five questions in this order. Could it see the future? What was it compared against, and how many times? Are the rungs of the ladder really the same book? Is the concentration measured in money? And who is missing from the data? A number that survives all five deserves attention. A number that has never been asked is just a number.

quiz.q: A backtest scores its signals using the whole history, then measures how those picks did. What's wrong?
a: It picked signals that turned out to work, then graded them — the answer was baked in before the test ran
quiz.why: Look-ahead: a decision made on a past Tuesday used information from after that Tuesday. Fixing it here dropped the headline win rate from about a half to about a third.

quiz.q: Your strategy beat a random comparison run. How much does that prove?
a: Very little on its own — one random run can land anywhere by chance; ask how many were run and where you sat in the spread
quiz.why: A single random run is an anecdote. Two hundred of them make a distribution, and 'above the 95th percentile' is a claim that means something.

quiz.q: On a slippage ladder, the 2% rung returns MORE than the 1.5% rung. What does that tell you?
a: The rungs aren't the same book — changing costs changed which shares got bought, so it isn't one dial being turned
quiz.why: Cost changes fill prices, which changes position sizes and slot timing, which changes the shares owned. Read the ladder as related experiments, not one strategy getting dearer.

quiz.q: Why report 'profit without the top three trades' in DOLLARS rather than as summed percentages?
a: Because a percentage says nothing about position size — and the dollar version still means something when the account lost money
quiz.why: A +400% gain on a small parcel can be a fifth of the money a +40% gain on a big one made. And a ratio against a negative total is undefined; dollars never are.

quiz.q: Every company in a ten-year test is still listed today. What does that do to the results?
a: Nothing — survivors are what you'd buy anyway
It makes them an upper bound: the failures were never in the data, so the test cannot lose money on a company that collapsed
quiz.why: Suspension and removal is the usual ending for a sub-$1 share. None of those are in the store, so every long-window figure flatters — treat it as the best case.

quiz.q: A signal shows an average edge of +0.30% per fire. Round-trip brokerage on your parcel is about 1.2%. Verdict?
a: A loser once the broker is paid — the edge doesn't clear the round trip
quiz.why: Costs come out of every trade. An edge below the round trip is a research curiosity, not a buy list — and half a ten-year honour roll failed exactly this test.
